$comment: Errors the audit finds, that are REAL, and that cannot be fixed yet.
Why this file exists: the audit exited FAIL on the same three orphan tables
every run for weeks. A permanently-red build is read exactly as often as a
warning list that is 87% noise -- which is to say, never -- and then a NEW
error lands in a red build nobody looks at. This course has lost two checks
An entry here does NOT mean the problem is acceptable. It means it is known,
it has a named gate, and the audit should stop shouting about it until that
gate lifts. Unacknowledged errors still FAIL.
The list is kept honest from BOTH ends:
- a new error that matches nothing here fails the audit
- an entry here that matches no current error ALSO fails the audit, as
stale. Otherwise this file becomes the place errors go to be forgotten,
which is the failure it was written to prevent.
`match` is a plain substring of the error text. Keep it short enough to
survive a recount -- match the table name, not 'queried in 2 lesson(s)'.
This file is HAND-WRITTEN. PROGRESS.md is the generated one.
$closed: Kept as a record of what this file was for, and of the one thing it held.
b6/0001 now defines the table, with the columns derived from what its
two consumers actually query: b7/0002 counts calls per token per day
for contact_limit, and b7/0003 ends live calls on revoke.
Two things that entry got right, and one it got wrong.
Right: the gate was real. What a call record persists genuinely was a
signalling question, and guessing at it in B2 would have produced a
table shaped like the wrong thing.
Right: the audit stayed green the whole time it was here, so the ERROR
that appeared the moment the table existed -- this entry going stale --
Wrong: the gate text said B6 'has not been written' long after b6/0001
was 961 lines long. Prose asserting something checkable went stale in
the file whose entire job is to stop that happening. Write a gate as a
condition to test, not as a status to remember.
